title: Vertical farming and the electricity bill

turns.speaker: Ward
turns.text: Another one went under last month. Third big vertical farm in two years.

turns.speaker: Elsa
turns.text: They were all built when electricity was cheap and money was free. Both of those stopped at once.

turns.speaker: Sunita
turns.text: That's the core of it. You're replacing sunlight, which is free, with electricity, which is not.

turns.speaker: Ward
turns.text: The pitch was always water and land savings, though, and those are genuine.

turns.speaker: Sunita
turns.text: They are. Ninety-odd per cent less water, a fraction of the land, no pesticide. None of which matters if the lighting cost exceeds the crop's value.

turns.speaker: Elsa
turns.text: Which is why it's all salad leaves and herbs. High value, low energy, short cycle.

turns.speaker: Elsa
turns.text: Nobody is growing wheat in a tower and nobody sensible ever claimed they would.

turns.speaker: Ward
turns.text: The claim was made quite a lot in the funding rounds, actually.

turns.speaker: Sunita
turns.text: By people raising money rather than by agronomists, which is a distinction worth keeping.

turns.speaker: Elsa
turns.text: Where it does work is somewhere with cheap power and expensive imports. Iceland, the Gulf, remote islands.

turns.speaker: Ward
turns.text: So it's a niche technology that was sold as a replacement for farming.

turns.speaker: Sunita
turns.text: And the backlash now overshoots the other way, which is a shame, because the niche is real.

turns.speaker: Elsa
turns.text: That's the usual arc. Oversold, dismissed, then quietly useful.

points: Several large vertical farms have failed, built when electricity and capital were cheap.
Sunita identifies the core problem as replacing free sunlight with purchased electricity.
Water, land and pesticide savings are genuine but irrelevant if lighting costs exceed crop value.
This restricts viable crops to high-value, low-energy salad leaves and herbs rather than staples.
Elsa notes viability where power is cheap and imports expensive, such as Iceland, the Gulf and remote islands.
They conclude the technology was oversold as a replacement for farming and is now dismissed too readily, though the niche is real.
